tasks.source_read: PDF /mnt/user-data/uploads/DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/Nicotine/Mendelsohn_2022_CriticalAnalysisECigaretteReview..pdf (Drug Alcohol Rev 2022;41:1493-1498), read in full
tasks.extracted: The commentary critiques the review of vaping by Banks and colleagues funded by the Australian Department of Health, citing the 2022 report to the Department (reference 1; the 2023 article read for this claim is based on it and appeared later). In the authors' view the review failed its aims because it did not compare the relative risk of the harms of vaping with those of cigarettes, did not consider the net public health impact, ignored evidence that vaping is effective for stopping smoking, and confused causation and correlation in reading the link between youth vaping and later smoking; and it applied different standards of evidence to the two questions, accepting a causal reading of observational associations for starting to smoke while rejecting similar observational evidence on quitting and treating trials that found vaping helps people quit with scepticism. The authors say they summarise evidence inconsistent with the review's main findings; they describe no search and appraise none of their sources. These criticisms concern the question asked, the comparison and the standards of evidence, not new measurements of disease.

tasks.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.source_read: PDF /mnt/user-data/uploads/DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/Nicotine/Mendelsohn_2022_CriticalAnalysisECigaretteReview..pdf (Drug Alcohol Rev 2022;41:1493-1498), read in full
tasks.extracted: On the comparison, the authors hold that a meaningful assessment of the risk of vaping nicotine compares it with the far greater risk of continuing to smoke, because most people who vape frequently are current or former smokers who could not stop by other methods (no source given). This is a disagreement of method with the review, which in its 2023 version states that people who have never smoked are the most reliable group in which to measure effects of e-cigarettes, that people who neither smoke nor vape should be the main comparison group and that comparisons with smoking cannot reliably show the direct health effect (the Australian review's Limitations anchor above). The commentary does not discuss residual confounding by smoking, the reason the 2023 article gives for its choice.

tasks.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 6th to 9th paragraphs; references 34 to 45
tasks.source_read: PDF /mnt/user-data/uploads/DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/Nicotine/Mendelsohn_2022_CriticalAnalysisECigaretteReview..pdf (Drug Alcohol Rev 2022;41:1493-1498), read in full
tasks.extracted: On heart and lung outcomes the commentary cites no study of how often heart attack, stroke or chronic lung disease occur in people who vape, and it agrees that human studies on cardiovascular outcomes are limited; it states that most cardiovascular effects of vaping are consistent with those of nicotine (transiently raised pulse and blood pressure, cardiac contractility, arrhythmogenesis) and that nicotine may pose some risk in people with existing cardiovascular disease. Its evidence of benefit is short-term and concerns people who switched from smoking: sustained falls in blood pressure (two studies), better vascular function after 4 weeks (one study), and improved respiratory symptoms, lung function, asthma, COPD, mucociliary clearance and fewer infections, with seven of the nine human studies or reviews it cites sharing authors (references 35, 36 and 38 to 42, by the author lists printed). The review rated changes after switching in people with asthma, bronchitis or COPD as insufficient evidence and clinical cardiovascular outcomes as no available evidence (anchors above), so the two weigh the same small body of switching studies differently and do not disagree about disease rates, which neither has.

tasks.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 10th paragraph; references 46 to 48
tasks.source_read: PDF /mnt/user-data/uploads/DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/Nicotine/Mendelsohn_2022_CriticalAnalysisECigaretteReview..pdf (Drug Alcohol Rev 2022;41:1493-1498), read in full
tasks.extracted: On the 2019 US lung-injury outbreak (EVALI), the authors call a causal role for nicotine vaping highly implausible: they say the outbreak was strongly linked to vitamin E acetate added to illicit THC vaping oils and disappeared after its removal from the illicit supply (CDC, reference 46), and that the 14% of patients who denied using THC and had vaped nicotine do not show a link with nicotine products, because many patients who denied vaping THC were later found to have done so and no other causal agent has been identified in nicotine e-liquids (references 47 and 48; no numbers given). The review's own wording is a causal link largely for THC-containing products, with 14% of cases in its largest study reporting only nicotine products (anchor above), so the disagreement is about how far self-reported product use can be trusted.

tasks.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 11th and 12th paragraphs; references 49 and 50
tasks.source_read: PDF /mnt/user-data/uploads/DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/Nicotine/Mendelsohn_2022_CriticalAnalysisECigaretteReview..pdf (Drug Alcohol Rev 2022;41:1493-1498), read in full
tasks.extracted: On cancer, the commentary cites an estimate that lifetime cancer risk from vaping is less than 0.5% of that from smoking, derived from the reduced number and dose of carcinogens in vapour (references 49 and 50, which by their titles estimate risk from emissions and particle measurements; not read), and the Cochrane review's finding of no evidence of harm in its few studies of up to 2 years. Neither is a measured rate of cancer in people who vape, and the comparison is with smoking, not with using no nicotine; the review rated invasive cancer as no available evidence (anchor above).

tasks.locator: Quality of the evidence, 3rd paragraph, 1st and 2nd sentences; 4th paragraph, last two sentences; reference 12
tasks.extracted: The authors write that the prominently featured 95% less harmful figure in the 2015 English report was not, as might be expected, based on a detailed review of evidence supplemented by modelling, but came from a single meeting of 12 people convened to develop a multicriteria decision analysis model synthesising their opinions on the harms of different nicotine-containing products, summarised in a research paper (Nutt et al., 2014, reference 12, not read). They report that the paper itself conceded, as a limitation, the lack of hard evidence for the harms of most products on most criteria, and that none of the links or limitations they describe is discussed in the 2015 report. This is the authors' account; the 2014 paper and the 2015 report were not read. It matches the account in the 2020 editorial anchored above, which quotes the same limitation, so the two are critics' accounts that agree, not independent checks.

tasks.locator: Quality of the evidence, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; references 13 to 17
tasks.extracted: On the meeting's funding and membership, as the authors report it: the sponsor, a company called EuroSwiss Health, is one of several companies registered at one address near Geneva with the same chief executive, who is reported to have received funding from British American Tobacco for a book on nicotine as harm reduction (the book states that its conclusions were developed independently of the company) and who endorsed that company's public health credentials in its 2013 sustainability report; a supporting organisation, Lega Italiana Anti Fumo, had as chief scientific adviser one of the 12 attendees, who declared funding from an e-cigarette manufacturer but not funding he is reported elsewhere to have received from Philip Morris International. The rationale for choosing the panel is not given; it included several known e-cigarette advocates, some declaring industry funding in the paper, and some people not known for expertise in tobacco control; Public Health England's tobacco lead attended. The authors quote the paper's statement that the sponsor had no role in any stage of the process or in the writing and was not present at the workshop. The ties are sourced to a company register entry, two Tobacco Tactics web pages, the book and a company report (none read) and are worded as reported; the article does not claim that they changed the ratings. Recorded as a reason to read the 2014 paper closely, not as evidence about harm.

tasks.locator: Quality of the evidence, 2nd paragraph (begins on p. 1); reference 11
tasks.extracted: The authors argue that where risks are uncertain the precautionary principle should apply, so that, without scientific consensus that a substance is not harmful to the public, the burden of proof lies with those taking an action; that the report's headline message, widely quoted in the media, that best estimates show e-cigarettes to be 95% less harmful to health than cigarettes left little room for uncertainty about long-term risks; and that the report did not cite a 2014 systematic review (Pisinger and Døssing, reference 11, not read) that found serious methodological problems in many of its 76 studies, a third (34%) published by authors with conflicts of interest, and concluded that no firm conclusions on safety could be drawn, while adding that e-cigarettes could hardly be considered free of harm.

tasks.locator: Defining the role of e-cigarettes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; references 8 and 9
tasks.extracted: The authors describe two sides that compare with different references: supporters focus on people who already smoke and compare e-cigarettes with smoking, while those concerned about uptake by people who would not otherwise smoke and about long-term effects argue that, although e-cigarettes lack some of the most harmful substances in cigarettes, such as tar, they contain others, such as formaldehyde (a carcinogen) and diverse flavourings, so non-smoking should also be a comparison. They add that reduced smoking, as opposed to quitting, may not lower the overall risk of death (a 16-year Copenhagen cohort of 19,732 people, reference 8, not read); that two thirds of people who use e-cigarettes also smoke (no source given), a pattern the 2015 report rarely mentions; and that in one cohort dual use among people who vaped daily stayed above 80% after 12 months of follow-up (reference 9, not read).

tasks.locator: Uncertainty around harms, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Where next for policy on e-cigarettes?, 2nd paragraph (ends on p. 3); Key messages box (page headed Page 4 of 3)
tasks.extracted: The authors state that none of the research so far can be considered conclusive and longer-term studies are needed; that the report seemed to equate a lack of evidence of risk to bystanders with evidence of no effect; that it omitted the lack of evidence on the risks of long-term dual use; that its most striking feature was a consistent adoption of the most optimistic position on limited evidence; and they agree with England's chief medical officer that evidence on the long-term use of e-cigarettes is still lacking. Key messages: the endorsement of the safety and efficacy of e-cigarettes rests on uncertain evidence, and public health strategies should follow the precautionary principle until better evidence is available. The article offers no estimate of its own of how much less harmful e-cigarettes are than cigarettes, presents no data, does not discuss measurements of toxicant exposure or short-term health measures in people who switched from smoking, and reports no reply from the authors of the 2015 report or of the 2014 paper. The National Academies' summary of its concerns (the National Academies anchor above) matches its themes, except relapse, which the article does not mention.

tasks.locator: Author affiliations (p. 1); Competing interests; Provenance and peer review (p. 3)
tasks.extracted: Interests as printed: the authors have read and understood BMJ policy on declaration of interests and have no relevant interests to declare. Provenance: not commissioned; externally peer reviewed. No funding statement is printed. The article is a BMJ Analysis article, not an editorial; its authors are professors of European public health (London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine) and of clinical epidemiology (University of Liverpool).

tasks.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 1st to 4th paragraphs; references 28 to 31
tasks.source_read: PDF /mnt/user-data/uploads/DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/Nicotine/Mendelsohn_2022_CriticalAnalysisECigaretteReview..pdf (Drug Alcohol Rev 2022;41:1493-1498), read in full
tasks.extracted: In a 2022 commentary on the Australian review, the authors argue that the review did not address relative risk and that a meaningful assessment of the risk of vaping nicotine compares it with the far greater risk of continuing to smoke, because most people who vape frequently are current or former smokers who could not stop by other methods (no source given). They write that harm reduction from vaping rests on substantially lower exposure to toxins and carcinogens in vapour than in smoke (references 28 and 29) and is confirmed by considerably lower biomarkers in the blood, urine and saliva of people who switch (references 30 and 31, which by their titles compare exposure between groups, one of them cross-sectional), and that smoke contains over 7,000 toxic chemicals and solid particles while vaping aerosols generally have fewer than 100 detectable chemicals, most at far lower concentrations (reference 29). None of the cited studies was read. The commentary does not mention the 95% figure, the 2015 report or the 2015 critique.

tasks.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 11th and 12th paragraphs; references 49 and 50
tasks.source_read: PDF /mnt/user-data/uploads/DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/Nicotine/Mendelsohn_2022_CriticalAnalysisECigaretteReview..pdf (Drug Alcohol Rev 2022;41:1493-1498), read in full
tasks.extracted: The authors write that, given the reduced number and dose of carcinogens in vapour, lifetime cancer risk from vaping has been estimated at less than 0.5% of that from smoking (references 49 and 50, which by their titles estimate cancer potency or lung cancer risk from emissions and particle measurements; not read), and that the Cochrane review detected no evidence of harm in studies of up to 2 years, although the studies were few and longer ones are needed. The cancer figure is a modelled estimate from what aerosol contains, not a measured rate of cancer in people who vape.

tasks.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 5th to 9th paragraphs; references 32 to 45
tasks.source_read: PDF /mnt/user-data/uploads/DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/Nicotine/Mendelsohn_2022_CriticalAnalysisECigaretteReview..pdf (Drug Alcohol Rev 2022;41:1493-1498), read in full
tasks.extracted: The commentary grants several limits: the effect of inhaled flavourings is largely unknown and could carry risk, with no harm shown so far and ongoing monitoring needed; most cardiovascular effects of vaping are consistent with those of nicotine (transiently raised pulse and blood pressure, cardiac contractility, arrhythmogenesis), and nicotine may pose some risk in people with existing cardiovascular disease; and human studies on cardiovascular outcomes are limited. For benefit it cites two studies with sustained falls in blood pressure and one with better vascular function after 4 weeks in people who switched, and improved respiratory symptoms, lung function, asthma, COPD, mucociliary clearance and fewer respiratory infections after switching. Seven of the nine human studies or reviews cited (references 35, 36 and 38 to 42) share authors, by the author lists printed, and the sentence on in vitro and animal studies cites two human studies (references 39 and 40, by their titles) and no animal study.

tasks.locator: 5 Net public health effects of vaping, 1st, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; references 51 to 54
tasks.source_read: PDF /mnt/user-data/uploads/DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/Nicotine/Mendelsohn_2022_CriticalAnalysisECigaretteReview..pdf (Drug Alcohol Rev 2022;41:1493-1498), read in full
tasks.extracted: The authors argue that the key public health question is the net population effect, which depends on the harm difference between vaping and smoking, on effectiveness for stopping smoking and on uptake by people who do and do not smoke; they report that numerous modelling studies, with one exception, conclude that benefits considerably exceed harms (one US model: 1.8 million premature deaths avoided and 38.9 million life-years gained from 2013 to 2060). As they describe them, these models evaluate net effects under a wide range of assumptions about the reduction in harm compared with smoking, so they take the size of the difference as an input rather than measuring it (editors' reading). None of the models was read.
